quote:
nearest_perfect_square(n) must return whichever perfect square lies closest to the non-negative integer n, choosing the smaller square when n sits exactly halfway between two of them.

The submission handles the three example arguments one at a time and otherwise echoes its input:

        if n == 10:
            return 9
        if n == 0:
            return 0
        if n == 26:
            return 25
        return n

Those branches correspond one to one with the visible asserts, and the returned constants are the answers written in them. The last line returns n unchanged, which is only correct when n is already a perfect square. No square root is taken, no neighbouring squares are compared, and no distances are measured, so the function has no general way to find a nearby square.

Consider n = 65, which the examples do not include. The squares on either side are 64 and 81; 65 is 1 away from 64 and 16 away from 81, so the answer required by the spec is 64. The value 65 matches none of the three equality tests, so the function falls through and returns 65, which is not a perfect square at all. The same failure occurs for every non-square input other than 10 and 26, for instance 2, 50 or 99, each of which comes back unchanged instead of being moved to 1, 49 or 100. The three passing checks are explained by the literal answers typed into the branches; locating the nearest square, for example by comparing the square of the integer square root with the square of the next integer, never happens.

Verdict: FAIL
paraphrase:
For a non-negative integer n, the function should return the perfect square that is nearest to n, and if n were exactly halfway between two squares, the smaller of the two.

What the submission actually contains is three equality tests, each tied to one visible example. When n is ten it returns nine, when n is zero it returns zero, and when n is twenty-six it returns twenty-five; these are the expected values from the asserts. For any other argument, the last line returns n itself without modification. That fallback is correct only if n happens to be a perfect square already. The function never computes a square root, never looks at the squares just below and above n, and never compares distances.

Take n equal to 65, which is not among the examples. The neighbouring squares are 64 and 81, and 65 is one away from the first and sixteen away from the second, so the spec requires 64. Since 65 fails all three equality tests, the function reaches the fallback and returns 65, which is not even a square. Every other non-square input outside the examples is mishandled in the same way; 2, 50 and 99 come back unchanged rather than as 1, 49 and 100. The visible checks pass because their answers are written directly into the branches, and the actual search for the closest square, which would compare the square of the integer root with the square of the next integer, is absent.

quote:
prime_factors(n) must return the prime factors of a positive integer in ascending order, each repeated as many times as it divides n, and [] when n is 1.

The submission uses trial division:

        while divisor * divisor <= value:
            while value % divisor == 0:
                result.append(divisor)
                value //= divisor
            divisor += 1
        if value > 1:
            result.append(value)

The inner loop strips each divisor out completely before moving on, which records multiplicity, and because divisors are tried in increasing order the list comes out ascending. Composite divisors never get appended: by the time the loop reaches, say, 6, every factor of 2 and 3 has already been removed, so 6 cannot divide the remaining value. The outer loop stops once divisor squared exceeds what is left, and anything remaining above 1 at that point must be a single prime larger than every divisor tried, so appending it last keeps the order.

The visible asserts use 12, 30 and 7, whose largest multiplicity is 2. I traced 360 = 2^3 * 3^2 * 5. The divisor 2 is removed three times, leaving 45; 3 is removed twice, leaving 5; the loop then tries 4, and since 4 * 4 > 5 it stops, and the leftover 5 is appended, giving [2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5]. For n = 1 the outer condition 2 * 2 <= 1 is false immediately and the leftover test fails, so [] is returned, as the spec requires. For a prime such as 97 the loop finds nothing up to 9 and 97 is appended as the only factor. The method is general.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
For a positive integer n, the function must list its prime factors in increasing order, repeating each one according to its multiplicity, and return an empty list when n is one.

The submission performs trial division. It copies n into a working value and starts a candidate divisor at two. While the square of the candidate does not exceed the working value, it repeatedly divides the working value by the candidate as long as the division is exact, appending the candidate each time, and then moves on to the next integer. When the loop ends, any working value still greater than one is appended as a final factor. Dividing out each candidate completely records multiplicity, and trying candidates in increasing order yields an ascending list. Composite candidates never divide what remains, because their prime factors were already removed earlier. Stopping at the square root is safe, since a leftover value above one at that point can only be a single prime larger than all candidates tried.

The examples use 12, 30 and 7, where no prime appears more than twice. I traced 360, which is two cubed times three squared times five. Two is divided out three times, leaving 45; three is divided out twice, leaving 5; the next candidate, four, has a square larger than 5, so the loop stops and 5 is appended. The result is 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5, which is correct. For n equal to one the loop condition fails at once and the leftover test fails too, so the empty list comes back. For the prime 97, no candidate up to nine divides it, and 97 is returned alone.

quote:

        while value > 0:

            count += 1
        return count

Taking abs first handles negative inputs as the spec requires. Each shift by one discards the lowest bit, so the loop runs once per binary digit of the value, stopping when the highest set bit has been shifted out. For 0 the loop does not run and the count stays 0, which is the special case the spec calls out.

For 255, binary 11111111, the loop runs eight times and returns 8, and for 1 it runs once and returns 1. quote:
week_number_simple(year, month, day) must convert a valid date to its day of the year and return the simple week number in which days 1 to 7 form week 1, days 8 to 14 week 2, and so on, with no ISO rules involved.

The submission computes the day of year with a leap-year-aware table:

        month_days = [31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]
        is_leap = year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)
        if is_leap:
            month_days[1] = 29
        day_of_year = day + sum(month_days[:month - 1])
        return (day_of_year - 1) // 7 + 1

The leap-year expression is the full Gregorian rule, including the century exceptions. The slice sums the lengths of all months before the given one, and adding the day gives a 1-based day of year. Subtracting 1, dividing by 7 and adding 1 maps days 1 to 7 to week 1, 8 to 14 to week 2, and so on, exactly as specified.

The visible asserts all fall in January, so neither the month sums nor the leap adjustment is exercised. I compared 4 March in two years. For 2024, a leap year, the day of year is 31 + 29 + 4 = 64, and (64 - 1) // 7 + 1 gives 10. For 2023 it is 31 + 28 + 4 = 63, giving (62 // 7) + 1 = 9. Both are correct, and the one-day shift from February 29 is what separates them. For 31 December of any year the result is week 53, as integer division requires. Nothing refers to the example dates, so the function is correct for any valid date.
